title: The Potter Who Invented Industrial Standardization
event_summary: In 1437, a Ming dynasty imperial kiln superintendent named Zhang Shanwu reorganized the massive porcelain workshops of Jingdezhen into a system of rigidly divided labor with 72 standardized production steps, each performed by specialist workers using calibrated tools and templates. Every bowl, plate, and vase emerging from the imperial kilns now had to match exact dimensional specifications enforced by government inspectors. This transformation turned Jingdezhen—a city of 300,000 people dedicated almost entirely to ceramics—into arguably the world's first assembly-line factory complex, producing over a million pieces annually for domestic and export markets.
why_forgotten: Western industrial history credits the division of labor to Adam Smith's pin factory example from 1776, roughly 340 years later, and the assembly line to Henry Ford. Chinese ceramic production was treated by European historians as exotic craft rather than industrial process. The administrative records of Jingdezhen's reorganization remained buried in Ming provincial archives and were only seriously examined by economic historians in the late twentieth century.
why_it_matters: The Jingdezhen system pioneered interchangeable parts, quality control inspection, and division of labor at a scale not seen in Europe for centuries, and its porcelain exports along maritime trade routes helped create the first truly global consumer commodity. Modern manufacturing's core principles—standardized specifications, specialized stations, and systematic quality assurance—were all operating in this Chinese city three centuries before the Industrial Revolution. The global appetite for Jingdezhen porcelain also drove the silver trade that connected the Americas, Europe, and Asia into a single world economy.
